To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
nuclear stress causes DNA damage and that lamin-A is required for nuclear stability.
nuclear envelope rupture is shared between lamin-A low cells and cells that migrate through narrow pores.
lamin-A low cells have increased nuclear rupture and DNA damage that is suppressed by growth on soft matrix or by lamin-A overexpression, which rescues the DNA repair factors.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how nuclear stress impacts DNA damage in lamin-A low cells, which is relevant to cancer and aging.
how nuclear stress affects the repair of DNA damage and is relevant for the study of cancer, aging and progeroid syndrome.
the mechanisms of how lamin-A mutations or lamin-A depletion cause DNA damage, which can result in cancer and other diseases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
nuclear stress in lamin-A low cells is associated with a loss of DNA repair factors that can be rescued by lamin-A re-expression or soft matrix, but not by the presence of a nuclear envelope.

lamin-A depletion in cells in 2D culture causes nuclear envelope rupture and loss of repair factors that are partially restored by soft matrix and that lamin-A depletion during 3D migration results in sustained loss of repair proteins.
the nuclear envelope rupture in cells with low lamin-A levels is associated with increased DNA damage.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
nuclear envelope rupture and repair factor mis-localisation under stress is a common theme in nuclear envelope biology that impacts DNA repair.
nuclear stress in stiff tissues and nuclear rupture during constricted migration cause similar mis-localization of nuclear proteins and DNA damage.

lamin-A is a critical factor for nuclear integrity and DNA repair factor localization, which is especially critical for the maintenance of nuclear structure and DNA integrity when the nuclear lamina is under stress from either constricted migration or from a rigid extracellular matrix.
The main takeaway from our work is that
lamin-A and DNA repair factors are important for the nuclear envelope and DNA repair in cells with stiff cytoskeleton, which is the most common cell type in the body.

the nuclear stress caused by constricted migration and lamin-A depletion in stiff tissues can cause mis-localization of repair factors and increased damage, which can be mitigated by lamin-A or by soft matrix.
nuclear envelope integrity is critical for DNA repair, which is compromised by both lamin-A depletion and 3D constrictive migration.
